courses.title: Meet your pieces
courses.description: Straight lines, diagonals and jumps. Learn how pieces reach their targets.

courses.title: Build a safe position
courses.description: Bring pieces into play, castle safely and collect loose material.

courses.title: Turn an idea into a move
courses.description: Use forks and pins, then make promotion work for you.

courses.title: Calculate the whole line
courses.description: Work through mating nets, deflections and pawn races from real games.

lessons.title: Rooks travel in straight lines
lessons.description: Use ranks and files to reach a target.
body: A rook moves along a rank or a file. It can travel several squares in one move, but cannot jump over another piece. When it captures, it stops on the occupied square.
Trace the whole path before moving. Both challenges ask you to capture a loose bishop with your rook. Check that the route is clear, and notice how the same rule works for either color.

challenges.title: Up the file
challenges.prompt: White to move. Capture the bishop on a7 with your rook.
challenges.explanation: Rxa7 takes the bishop at the end of a clear file.

challenges.title: Down the file
challenges.prompt: Black to move. Capture the bishop on h2 with your rook.
challenges.explanation: Rxh2 follows the h-file and captures the bishop. Board orientation does not change how a rook moves.

lessons.title: Bishops follow diagonals
lessons.description: Find the diagonal that connects attacker and target.
body: A bishop moves diagonally and stays on squares of one color for the whole game. Like a rook, it cannot jump over a piece. Look at each square between the bishop and its target.

A bishop can take a more valuable piece if it can reach it safely. These exercises focus on finding a legal diagonal capture; they are examples of movement, not a complete evaluation of every possible continuation.

challenges.title: A long diagonal
challenges.prompt: White to move. Capture the rook on g5 with your bishop.
challenges.explanation: Bxg5 follows c1–d2–e3–f4–g5 and takes the rook.

challenges.title: The other direction
challenges.prompt: Black to move. Capture the rook on b4 with your bishop.
challenges.explanation: Bxb4 follows the diagonal through e7, d6 and c5.

lessons.title: Knights can jump
lessons.description: Reach a square that sliding pieces cannot.
body: A knight moves two squares along a rank or file and then one square sideways. Its destination is always the opposite color from its starting square. Pieces between the start and destination do not block it.
Only the destination decides whether the knight captures. In each position your own pawns occupy the nearby rank, but the knight can jump over them to capture the rook.

challenges.title: Jump from b1
challenges.prompt: White to move. Use the knight to capture the rook on c3.
challenges.explanation: Nxc3 jumps over the nearby pawns and captures on its destination.

challenges.title: Jump from g8
challenges.prompt: Black to move. Use the knight to capture the rook on f6.
challenges.explanation: Nxf6 is a knight jump. The pawns on the seventh rank do not block it.

lessons.title: Castle with a safe king
lessons.description: Move king and rook together when the conditions are right.
body: Castling moves the king two squares toward a rook, then puts the rook on the square the king crossed. The king and that rook must retain castling rights, and the squares between them must be empty.

The king cannot castle out of check, through check or into check. A rook being attacked is not itself a ban. These prepared positions have a legal route; make the specified castle and watch both pieces move.

challenges.title: Castle kingside
challenges.prompt: White to move. Castle kingside by moving the king to g1.
challenges.explanation: O-O moves the king to g1 and the rook to f1.

challenges.title: Castle queenside
challenges.prompt: Black to move. Castle queenside by moving the king to c8.
challenges.explanation: O-O-O moves the king to c8 and the rook to d8. The b8 square also had to be empty.

lessons.title: Bring both knights into play
lessons.description: Build a position instead of moving one piece repeatedly.
body: Developing a piece means bringing it into useful play. Knights near the center can influence more squares than knights stuck on a corner. Development is a habit, not a rule that overrides immediate threats.

Practice one simple sequence: develop the kingside knight toward the center, observe the opponent’s knight reply, then develop the queenside knight. Many other opening moves are playable; this lesson follows the named development plan.

challenges.title: Develop White’s knights
challenges.prompt: Play Nf3. After Black develops a knight, play Nc3.
challenges.explanation: Both white knights now influence central squares. The displayed reply is one example, not a forced response.

challenges.title: Develop Black’s knights
challenges.prompt: Black to move in this practice setup. Play Nf6, then Nc6 after the reply.
challenges.explanation: Both black knights have joined the game. Continue checking the opponent’s threats as you develop.

lessons.title: Notice the loose piece
lessons.description: Look for useful captures before choosing a quiet move.
body: An undefended piece can be a tactical opportunity. Before taking it, check whether the move is legal and whether the opponent has a reply that changes the material balance.
Pawns move forward but capture one square diagonally forward. Here a pawn can collect a loose rook. Compare the board after the capture rather than just noticing that two pieces were near each other.

challenges.title: White’s diagonal capture
challenges.prompt: Capture the black rook on e4 with the d3 pawn.
challenges.explanation: dxe4 removes the loose rook and leaves the white pawn on e4.

challenges.title: Black’s diagonal capture
challenges.prompt: Capture the white rook on d5 with the e6 pawn.
challenges.explanation: exd5 follows Black’s forward direction and captures the rook.

lessons.title: Create two threats
lessons.description: A checking fork gives the opponent an urgent problem.
body: A fork attacks two targets with one piece. A checking fork is especially useful because the opponent must first make the king safe. The other target may then be available to capture.

Find a knight check that also attacks the queen. After the demonstrated king reply, collect the queen. Other legal king replies can exist; the lesson teaches one verified continuation rather than claiming the opponent has only one move.

challenges.title: White’s checking fork
challenges.prompt: Find Ne7+, then capture the queen after the king reply.
challenges.explanation: Ne7+ attacks the king and queen. After Kf7, Nxd5 collects the queen.

challenges.title: Black’s checking fork
challenges.prompt: Find Ne2+, then capture the queen after the king reply.
challenges.explanation: Ne2+ attacks the king on g1 and queen on d4. After Kf2, Nxd4 takes the queen.

lessons.title: A pinned piece can still capture
lessons.description: Stay on the line protecting your king.
body: An absolute pin stops a piece from leaving a line when doing so would expose its king. This does not always make the piece immobile: it may move along the line or capture the attacker if the king stays safe.
The rooks in these positions face each other along the e-file, with your king behind your rook. Capture the pinning rook. The move removes the attacker without exposing your king.

challenges.title: Capture along the pin
challenges.prompt: White to move. Use the rook on e2 to capture the rook on e8.
challenges.explanation: Rxe8 removes the pinning rook. Moving off the e-file would have exposed the king.

challenges.title: The pin from Black’s side
challenges.prompt: Black to move. Use the rook on e7 to capture the rook on e1.
challenges.explanation: Rxe1 keeps the king safe by removing the line attacker.

lessons.title: Promote with a plan
lessons.description: Choose the piece after checking the resulting position.
body: When a pawn reaches the last rank, it must become a queen, rook, bishop or knight as part of that move. Usually a queen is useful, but the resulting position matters more than the piece’s nominal value.

In the second challenge, c8=Q would leave Black with no legal move while not in check: stalemate. Promoting to a rook keeps a legal black king move available. Use the requested rook promotion and compare the squares it controls.

challenges.title: Choose a queen
challenges.prompt: White to move. Advance the a-pawn and promote to a queen.
challenges.explanation: a8=Q records the chosen promotion piece as part of the move.

challenges.title: Avoid stalemate
challenges.prompt: White to move. Promote the c-pawn to a rook, not a queen.
challenges.explanation: c8=R leaves Black the a6 square. c8=Q would cover that escape and cause stalemate.

lessons.title: Calculate a mating net
lessons.description: Follow checks until every escape is covered.
body: A mating net works when checking pieces and supporting pieces cover the king’s remaining escapes. Do not stop calculating after the first check: ask where the king can go and which defender can intervene.

lessons.title: Remove a defender
lessons.description: See what a defender stops protecting when it moves.
body: Deflection draws a defending piece away from a task. A forcing move can make an attractive capture possible later. Track both the immediate check or threat and the piece that becomes vulnerable.

In these source examples, follow the forcing continuation and count what is removed from the board. A sacrifice is not justified just because it is forcing; the resulting position and the defender’s alternatives still matter.

lessons.title: Calculate a pawn race
lessons.description: Count king moves as carefully as pawn moves.
body: In a pawn ending, one tempo can decide whether a pawn promotes, is caught or forces a concession. Count moves for both sides and include king captures, not only the number of squares to promotion.

These examples ask you to calculate a complete local source line. One includes a promotion that is immediately captured; the other activates the king toward queenside pawns. Do not assume a promotion ends the calculation.
